Denali is North America's highest peak at twenty thousand three hundred ten feet, located in the Alaska Range of interior Alaska, approximately one hundred thirty miles north of Anchorage. Formerly called Mount McKinley after the twenty-fifth U.S. President, it was officially renamed Denali in two thousand fifteen, an Athabascan word meaning the great one. Despite its lower altitude than many global mountains, Denali is considered exceptionally challenging due to its remote location, extreme cold, and the dramatic elevation gain from sea level. The brief climbing season runs from May through July. Winter temperatures plummet to minus forty Fahrenheit with wind chills far lower, and climbers face crevasse fields, avalanche danger, and acute cold injury. The mountain is remote and accessible primarily by bush plane or foot. Hudson Stuck and his party made the first ascent in nineteen thirteen, though Indigenous peoples and earlier explorers had traversed the region. Denali is considered a crucial training ground for Himalayan mountaineering. Many Everest climbers summit Denali first to test high-altitude acclimatization and logistics. The Rescue Bowl phenomenon occurs when weather can trap climbers for weeks, demanding patience and respect.
